rv.q: Less butterfly, more caterpillar.
But Julie Taymor’s staging and Hwang’s rewrites unbalance the delicate poise between illusion and truth.
Three decades later, M. Butterfly remains provocative and timely, with a great deal to unpack.
Dramatic love story still resonates.
Jin Ha and Clive Owen bring fresh intensity to this revival of David Henry Hwang's Tony-winning drama.

Here, Owen seems more deeply haunted by Gallimard's forbidden love for Song Liling (a lithe Jin Ha in this production); but his earnest attempt to play the character's sexual uncertainty is ultimately unconvincing.
Owen and Ha are doing their best to anchor M. Butterfly, but like its namesake, the show often seems to be floating just above something truly powerful, looking for a place to land.
Otherwise, the production is mired in an indecisive middle.
The crux of M. Butterfly, the beauty and cruelty of Gallimard and Song’s knotty relationship, never fully takes flight.
But in their counterintuitive attempt to make the play relevant for an audience more versed in the complexities of gender and racial politics, Taymor and Hwang have inadvertently undercut its pathos.
In this incarnation, we’re not being seduced, but preached at.
But the story is just as silly as the opera.

M. Butterfly has proven its relevance into the Wikipedia era — you can look up the particulars on your phone at intermission if you’re so inclined — but its greater enduring value is as a thought-provoking fable.
You are just not going to find a director more willing to take an artistic risk on the American stage than Julie Taymor and here the all risks pay off.
This is a fantastic performance by the former NYU Tisch Graduate

Minor quibbles about the play's occasionally sluggish pace shouldn't obscure the point that no other Broadway director comes close to Taymor's magpie talent for incorporating diverse theatrical forms into a singular vision.
Go to this 'M. Butterfly' with an open mind. Even if it doesn't add up to quite the 'wow' you saw or heard about, you'll find it to still be an intriguingly unusual and enormously theatrical story.
In a country that is so steeped in racist beliefs, this revival of “M. Butterfly” is a political act, boldly challenging its audience to no longer accept intolerance, stigmatization, or stereotypes.
In fact, you may find yourself wishing the Cort had provided seat belts, because if your fondness for the original runs high, your feelings may be in for a very bumpy night.
Even for some of us who did, the new “M Butterfly,” for all its changes, remains provocative, enlightening and entertaining.

If David Henry Hwang's latter career has been less than stellar, M. Butterfly still packs a wallopeven, as it turns out, in a production that features a wan performance in one of the two central roles, and even though the element of surprise has inevitably been lost over the decades.
The result is occasionally striking but ultimately disappointing from the director of The Lion King and a dazzling Midsummer Night’s Dream.
So strong is Hwang's writing, "M. Butterfly" is riveting theatre, even when the production fails to fully take wing.
In his rewritten play, Hwang has so much going on that it’s difficult to say for sure what’s going on, and sometimes that includes the plot.
She keeps the play focused on the tragedy of the concept of discrimination, instead of the pain and humanity of the characters.
Try as everyone might, this “Butterfly” never really soars; but it rarely crashes to the ground either.
While not much is wrong with this production, we couldn’t help but yearn for the magical theatricality of its first version.
As Gallimard, the usually suave and masculine Owen has chosen to play him as awkward, though he seems less a man uncomfortable in his own skin than an actor who hasn’t found the center of his role.

With a revised plot for this Broadway revival, the production by director Julie Taymor unfortunately leans towards flatness and simplicity which dulls the power of the play and muddies the play’s intentions.
Basic to M. Butterfly is the duality basic to all theater — people pretending to be other people — a pleasure largely lost in the surprisingly dull revival.

The original script is a solid piece of construction leavened by considerable wit and ideas that still provoke and stimulate; by adding all this froufrou, a once-powerful drama now packs all the sting of, well, a butterfly.
Between a wan star turn, a clumsy staging and nagging issues that remain even with a revised script, the revival at the Cort Theatre frustrates and falls flat.
The play was ripe for revival — and it has instead been ripped apart.
His final descent into Jean Genet levels of sexual panic and identity loss is arresting and raw.
Julie Taymor’s onslaught is straight on powerful and direct, energetically engaging, and dramatically concise.
It's a testament to this revival that a play set in the '60s, and first staged in the '80s, can still offer compelling questions about where we're going.
Huang's rewriting and Taymor's staging deviate from the fine-spun illusion of mystery and culture.
It’s not a must-see since it is woefully dated, but the performances are worth either seeing it for the first time or seeing it again.
The stunning albeit straightforward play about fantasy, deception, espionage, and betrayal seems to have lost its way
Butterfly is an enthralling play that’s lost none of its luster over time.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this revival, with critics finding Hwang's play dated and Taymor's staging uneven, though some praise the performances and timely themes of gender and cultural identity.

sg.ra: JEJ is one of Broadway's smallest houses (1,063-1,092 seats across sources) and seats 101-112 in Center Orch rows AA-A put you almost nose-to-stage; SeatPlan and Headout both name seats 105-109 in AA-A as the single best spots. Mezz overhang doesn't bite until Row J, so Center Orch stays clean of ceiling cutoff all the way back to Row I.

SeatPlan explicitly calls out 'Rows E to J in the Center Orchestra are cheaper than premium with a good view,' and because JEJ's auditorium is unusually compact even Row J sits closer to the stage than mid-orch in bigger Shubert houses. This is the sweet spot before the Mezz overhang obscures the top of the stage (SeatPlan: cuts in after Row O; TickPick: overhang begins Row J but worsens deeper).

sg.vl: Overview pick with an elevated head-on
sg.ra: JEJ Mezz is one of Broadway's smallest (264-275 seats) and sits directly above the stage per SeatPlan: 'every row facing directly above the stage.' SeatPlan notes the Balcony overhang at Mezz Row B 'doesn't affect views' and the railing height doesn't obstruct (TickPick). Good rake means heads-in-front is a non-issue. AVFMS April 2024: 'View was fantastic, person in front didn't obstruct my view.'

sg.vl: Underrated value if you skew center
sg.ra: Unusual for Broadway, TickPick explicitly states JEJ 'does not have obstructed view seats on the sides of the orchestra and mezzanine' thanks to the small footprint and no pillars. But SeatPlan warns double-digit seats at the far side and Boxes above 16 are angled with stage right partially obstructed, so you want the low-numbered seats closer to center aisle.
sg.rr: L Mezz A-G odd 1-25; R Mezz A-G even 2-26; plus 24 box seats

sg.vl: Cheapest tier, steepest price in comfort
sg.ra: SeatPlan: Balcony is 'very steep and cramped compared to the lower two seating areas,' ~2 steps down per row with three flights of stairs (Shubert: 55 steps total or elevator post-renovation). SeatPlan flags Row H as 'isn't as well-raked as the rest of the section,' so the back row both loses rake AND inherits the steep climb. JEJ balcony is unusually high — Shubert's own description puts it behind Row F entrance.
sg.rr: A-G (L/R) / A-H (Center); 283 seats plus 12 box seats
